blocks.text: What is it?

Cyber hygiene is the set of small, regular habits that keep your phone, accounts, money and personal data safe — just as washing hands keeps germs away. It is not a one-time setting; it is a routine. Most frauds in India do not “hack” a system. They trick a person into giving away an OTP, a PIN, a password or access to a phone. Good habits close those doors before anyone knocks.

Key term            Figure 1.3 · Six everyday risks that cyber hygiene protects against Cyber hygiene           Meaning Social engineering      Simple, regular habits that protect devices, accounts and personal data Phishing                Tricking people with urgency, fear or greed instead of breaking technology A fake message, call or website that pretends to be trusted in order to steal details

A shopping site Ravi once used was breached. Criminals tried his leaked email and password on Instagram and Gmail — they worked, because he used the same password everywhere. Within an hour his friends received “urgent” requests for money from his account. Lesson: one reused password turned one leak into three takeovers. Unique passphrases and two-step verification would have stopped it.
Ask yourself

items: Am I careful when clicking links, downloading files or sharing information online?
Do I use the same password for more than one important account?
Is two-step verification on for my WhatsApp, email and banking apps?

What is it?

A weak password is short or personal (a name, a birth year, 12345678). A strong one is long, random and used for only one account. A passphrase of four random words is both strong and easy to remember. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second check after the password: a code from an app, a prompt on your phone, a passkey or a fingerprint. Even if a password leaks, the account stays locked.

What is it?

Your phone holds bank apps, photos, contacts and OTPs. Device security rests on four building blocks: a screen lock, updates, apps from trusted sources only, and minimum permissions. A permission is an app's request to use the camera, microphone, contacts, location, SMS or files. Give each app only what it needs to do its job. An app installed from a link (an APK file) can read OTPs and mirror your screen.

What is it?

Personal information identifies you (name, phone, address, date of birth, photos). Sensitive information can cause serious harm if misused (Aadhaar, PAN, bank details, health records). Your digital footprint is everything about you online — what you post, what others post and what apps collect. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, you have the right to know how your data is used, to correct it, to ask for its erasure and to complain to the organisation and then the Data Protection Board.

Neha posted a week-long holiday with live location while her house in Pune stood empty. A neighbour's CCTV later showed strangers checking the door. Lesson: share trips after you return, switch off live location on posts, and keep the account private.
Your digital footprint can stay online for years. Think before you share, and share sensitive documents only in masked form and only for a verified need.
What is it?

Safe internet use is about where you connect, what you click and what you keep a copy of. A fake website looks exactly like the real one; the difference is in the address and in how you arrived there.

blocks.text: Role limits

A First Responder identifies, stabilises, preserves and routes. Complex or high-risk cases go to the police, the bank, CERT-In (for organisations) or other authorised professionals. This is covered in depth in Modules 4 to 6.
HOW ONLINE FRAUDS WORK
What is it?

An online fraud is a trick that uses a phone, app, website or message to make a person give away money, details or access. Almost every fraud is social engineering: it targets feelings — fear, greed, urgency, trust or kindness — rather than technology. Once you know the pattern, you can spot a scam you have never seen before.
Why money disappears so fast

UPI and IMPS move money in seconds, at any hour. Fraudsters pass it through several mule accounts — accounts rented or opened in other people's names — and withdraw it as cash or crypto. Reporting on 1930 lets banks place a hold on money still in those accounts; every minute of delay lets more of it leave.
What is it?

Phishing is a fake message, email or website that pretends to come from a trusted organisation — a bank, electricity company, courier, tax department or employer — to steal login details, card numbers or OTPs, or to make you install a harmful app. Smishing is phishing by SMS; vishing is by voice call.

“Refund approved; verify your account”  Refunds go to the account already in your tax profile; no link is needed

Sunita received an SMS saying her bank reward points would expire today. The link opened a page that looked exactly like her bank. She entered her customer ID, password and then the OTP. Within minutes, ₹48,000 was transferred out. Lesson: the page address ended in a different domain, and the bank's real app would never ask for an OTP to “redeem points”. Opening the official app, instead of the link, would have stopped the loss.
Ask yourself

items: Did I expect this message, and does it create a deadline or a threat?
Does the link's real owner (read right to left) match the organisation?
Is it asking for a login, OTP, card number or an app install?

blocks.save: Screenshot the message showing sender, link and time.

blocks.text: Never open a bank, tax or utility service from a link in a message. Type the address yourself or use the official app.

2.title: UPI, QR code and OTP frauds

blocks.text: What is it?

UPI is safe when you understand one rule: the UPI PIN authorises money to leave your account. Fraudsters invent stories that make you enter it while believing you will receive money — a refund, a prize, an advance payment or a “wrong transfer” to return.

Arjun listed his old sofa online. A “buyer” said he was being transferred and would send ₹10,000 in advance. He sent a QR code and said, “Scan and enter your PIN to receive.” ₹10,000 left Arjun's account. The “buyer” said it was a mistake and asked him to try again. Lesson: you never scan a code or enter a PIN to receive money. Stop at the first request.
Shopkeepers: protect your QR

Use separate UPI IDs or accounts for business and savings, and set daily limits.

3.title: Fake bank, KYC and customer-care frauds

blocks.text: What is it?

The caller says your KYC has expired, your card will be blocked, or you have a pending reward. Or you search online for a company's helpline and call a fake number placed by fraudsters. Either way, the “executive” asks for card details or OTP, or asks you to install a screen-sharing or remote-access app so they can “help”. RBI and banks repeatedly warn: no bank employee will ask for your PIN, OTP, CVV or password, or ask you to install a remote-access app. KYC is updated through the branch, the official app or the official website.

What is it?

These scams use greed or fear. Task-based job scams pay small amounts for liking videos or rating hotels, then demand ever-larger “investments”. Investment scams add victims to WhatsApp or Telegram “stock tips” groups and fake trading apps showing false profits. In a digital arrest scam, callers pose as police, CBI, customs or narcotics officers on video and keep the victim on camera until money is paid.

Kavya earned ₹150 for liking three videos and was moved to a Telegram group of “earners”. Over four days she paid ₹1.8 lakh in “merchant tasks”. Her dashboard showed ₹3 lakh, but withdrawal needed a 20% “tax”. Lesson: a job that asks you to pay is not a job.

Fraudsters pretend to be someone you trust: a relative in trouble abroad, a friend whose WhatsApp has been taken over, a senior officer, a soldier buying your goods. What is it?

The golden hour is the first hour after a fraudulent transaction. A call to the 1930 helpline (run under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, MHA) sends the details to banks and payment apps so they can try to hold the money before it leaves mule accounts. The complaint is then completed on cybercrime.gov.in (the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, NCRP).

blocks.text: What is it?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that learns patterns from very large amounts of data and then uses those patterns to predict, sort or create. Generative AI creates new content — a paragraph, a picture, a song or a video — from a short instruction. A deepfake is a photo, video or audio clip made or altered with AI so that a real person seems to say or do something they never did. The word joins “deep learning” (the AI method) and “fake”.

In early 2024, an employee of a multinational firm's Hong Kong office joined a video call with people who looked and sounded like the company's finance chief and colleagues. On their instructions he made a series of transfers worth about US$25 million. Every other person on the call was a deepfake. Lesson: seeing a familiar face on a live call is no longer proof. Large or unusual requests must be confirmed through a separate, known channel.
The technology is neutral. Consent, labelling and intent make the difference between creative work and a crime.
What is it?

AI can now produce a photograph of a person who does not exist, swap one face onto another in a video, make a real person's lips match new words (lip-sync), and clone a voice from a short sample so that it can say anything typed into it. Some clues can reveal manipulation, especially in quickly made fakes. But tools improve every month, and a good fake may show no clue at all. Clues raise suspicion; they do not prove anything either way.

What is it?

Impersonation means pretending to be someone else — through a fake profile using their photos, a hijacked account, or AI media of their face or voice. Morphing is editing a person's photo, often onto a sexual image, to shame or blackmail them. Sextortion is threatening to share intimate or morphed images unless the victim pays or sends more images. The person shown is a victim, whether the image is real or fake. Shame keeps victims silent, which is exactly what the criminal relies on.

What the law and platforms provide

Under the IT Rules 2021, platforms must act on a complaint about intimate or morphed images of a person within 24 hours. Publishing such material is an offence under the IT Act 2000 (ss. 66E, 67, 67A; s. 67B for children) and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023; impersonation online is an offence under IT Act s. 66D. Child sexual material is reported at once; it is never copied or viewed (Modules 5 and 7).

Ayesha, 22, received a message with a morphed image made from her public Instagram photos and a demand for ₹5,000. A friend trained as a First Responder told her it was not her fault, helped her save the account link and chat, used StopNCII to create a hash of the image on her own phone, reported the account and filed on cybercrime.gov.in. The account was removed; no payment was made.

What is it?

Verification is a routine, not a feeling. The S·I·F·T routine — Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace to the original — works on photos, videos, voice notes and headlines alike. The honest result is one of three verdicts: genuine, fake, or cannot verify yet.

blocks.text: Responsible AI: the consent rule

Creating AI images, video or voice of a real person without their consent can violate their privacy and dignity and may be an offence. Under the DPDP Act 2023, a person's image and voice are personal data. Label AI-generated content you share, never use AI to sexualise, mock or impersonate a real person, and never feed someone else's private photos into an AI tool.

0.title: What triage is, and your role

blocks.text: What is it?

Triage comes from hospital emergency rooms: patients are seen in order of danger, not in order of arrival. Cyber triage does the same with incidents. A ₹500 debit that is happening now is more urgent than a ₹2 lakh loss from last month, because the first can still be stopped. A Community Cyber First Responder is the first trained person a citizen meets. Their job is to identify what is happening, stabilise it, preserve what matters and route the case to the agency that can act — and to stay with it until the hand-over is confirmed.

Grade urgency and explain the reason
Contact, bait or threaten the suspect

Promise a freeze, refund or arrest

blocks.text: Preserve identifiers and records (Module 5)
Route to police, bank, telecom, platform or IT lead (Module 6)

At a community help desk, Mr Rao arrives first: he lost ₹2 lakh in an investment scam three weeks ago. Five minutes later Sunita arrives: her phone lost signal this morning and ₹18,400 has just been debited. A trained responder apologises to Mr Rao, helps Sunita call her bank and 1930 immediately, and then returns to Mr Rao's case, which still needs a complaint the same day. Lesson: urgency follows present danger and active loss. Both cases matter; one cannot wait.
What is it?

Digital evidence is any record that helps establish what happened: chats, call logs, bank messages and statements, emails, web addresses (URLs), profile IDs, app details, photos of a screen, and device information. blocks.text: What is it?

The evidence register is a simple table with one row per item. The chain of custody is the record of every person who has held the item, when and why. Together they let anyone check that the evidence is complete and has not been tampered with.

blocks.text: What is it?

A hash is a fixed-length “fingerprint” calculated from a file. SHA-256 is a widely used hash method. If even one dot of the file changes, the hash changes completely. Recording the hash of the master copy lets anyone later show that a working copy is identical.

Hash the master once, record it, and never open the master for editing. Compare hashes whenever a copy changes hands.

Some evidence is itself harmful. Copying or forwarding intimate images re-victimises the person, and possessing or sharing child sexual abuse material is a serious offence even when the intention is to help. For such material the First Responder preserves only identifiers — links, usernames, platform and time — and reports.

A First Responder does not give legal advice, but should be able to explain, in a sentence, which laws protect the citizen and what rights they have. The new criminal laws — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) — replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act from 1 July 2024.

blocks.text: What is it?

Cyber-crime is often treated as “just money” or “just online”. For victims it can feel like a burglary of the mind: someone they trusted turned out to be a criminal, private images may be seen by others, and family savings may be gone. Many victims blame themselves and hide what happened. Secondary victimisation is harm caused by the reaction of others — family, police, bank staff or helpers — through blame, disbelief or insensitive questions. A First Responder's first job is to make sure it does not happen at their desk.

1.title: Psychological first aid: look, listen, link

blocks.text: What is it?

Psychological first aid (PFA) is humane, supportive and practical help for people in distress. It is not counselling or therapy, and it never forces people to talk about what happened. Its three action principles are Look (for safety, urgent needs and severe reactions), Listen (to needs and concerns, and help people feel calm) and Link (to practical help, information, loved ones and services).

Active listening skill          Figure 7.5 · What to say — and what to avoid Attending               What it looks like Reflecting feelings     Face the person; put your phone away; nod; allow silence Summarising             “It sounds like you feel embarrassed and worried about your family.” Open questions          “So the call came at 10, you paid twice, and now he wants more. Is that right?” Respecting pace         “What happened next?” rather than “Did you give him the OTP?” in an accusing tone Let the person stop; return to practical steps when they are ready
Ask yourself

Did any of my words sound like blame?
Did I offer choices rather than take over?

What is it?

Sextortion, large financial loss and online abuse can push people into crisis. A First Responder must notice the warning signs and act at once. Safety overrides every other part of the case — evidence, forms and reports can wait.

Reporting is a legal duty under POCSO s.19. Do not question the child repeatedly; let trained officers do that. Involve a parent or guardian unless they may be the source of harm.
Ask directly about safety. Stay. Connect. Never keep a risk to life secret.

Trauma-informed support means assuming that the person may be affected by trauma and avoiding anything that re-traumatises them. Five principles guide every conversation. Then the message is adapted to the listener — the same next step may need different words, pace and format.

A citizen's story, identity and evidence belong to them. blocks.text: Mr Thomas received a WhatsApp message from an unknown number: “Wedding invitation — open the card”. The file was an APK. After installing it, his phone began forwarding SMS to the criminals. That night, OTPs were used to add his card to a payment wallet and ₹62,000 was spent. Lesson: an invitation is a picture or PDF, never an app. Any file ending in .apk sent on chat is a red flag.
What is it?

Compromise rarely announces itself, except in ransomware. Most signs are small: OTPs you did not request, a phone that heats up while idle, a recovery email that has changed. One sign is a reason to check carefully; several together call for isolation.

Email forwarding rules: after taking over an email account, criminals often add a rule that silently forwards bank and security emails to themselves — and keep it even after the password is changed. Check the email settings for forwarding and filters.

Isolation cuts the attacker's connection to the device; preservation keeps the device as it is so that the police or IT lead can examine it. Both are done in the first ten minutes. The instinct to reset, uninstall or run a “cleaner” app must be resisted until the case has been routed.

When an account has been taken over, recovery must be done from a clean device — one the attacker has never controlled — using official recovery routes. blocks.text: Why the email account comes first
Most other accounts reset their passwords by email. If the attacker still controls the email, they can take back everything else. Secure the email first, then the accounts that depend on it.

In a SIM swap, a criminal gets a new SIM issued for the victim's number — by fraud at a store or by tricking the victim into a “SIM upgrade” — and then receives all OTPs. A banking trojan reads OTPs and screens directly on the victim's phone. Both often come together with a hijacked email account. The sign is a phone that suddenly shows “No Service”, or OTPs and debits the person did not initiate.

5.title: Ransomware in small organisations, and prevention

blocks.text: What is it?

Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment. Schools, clinics, shops and small offices are frequent victims because they often lack backups and IT staff. The First Responder's job is to contain, escalate and record — never to negotiate, pay or attempt decryption.
Rules every First Responder should know

items: Organisations such as service providers, intermediaries, data centres, companies and government bodies must report specified cyber incidents, including ransomware, to CERT-In within 6 hours of noticing them (CERT-In directions, 2022). Citizens and small organisations can also report to CERT-In.
No More Ransom (nomoreransom.org), a law-enforcement and industry project, offers free decryption tools for some ransomware families; the IT lead checks it.
Cyber Swachhta Kendra (csk.gov.in), run by CERT-In, provides free tools and advice to clean infected devices.

What is it?

IoT devices are ordinary objects with an internet connection: cameras, TVs, speakers, watches, plugs, doorbells, baby monitors. OT systems control physical processes: a society's water pump, a rooftop solar inverter, a lift, a fire alarm. Both are computers, but they are rarely treated as computers — so they are rarely updated or secured.

Setting                                  Figure 9.3 · A typical connected home Home                        Common connected devices School                      Router, smart TV, camera, smart speaker, doorbell, children's smartwatch, fitness band Shop or clinic              Classroom displays, CCTV, biometric attendance, Wi-Fi access points, lab computers Housing society or village  CCTV, billing PC, POS terminal, UPI sound-box, medical devices, router Water-pump controller, gate access, intercom, solar inverter, lifts
What is it?

Most smart-device attacks need no special skill. Lists of default usernames and passwords are public, and automated programs scan the internet for devices that still use them. In 2016, the Mirai botnet took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and video recorders with default passwords and used them to knock major websites offline.
If a device came with a password printed on a sticker, change it the day you install it.

2.title: Securing the home or shop router

blocks.text: What is it?

The router is the front door of every device behind it. Two passwords matter: the Wi-Fi password that devices use to join, and the admin password that opens the router's settings page. Many routers supplied by internet providers still use a default admin password.

If the router belongs to the internet provider
Ask the provider to change the admin password or update firmware if you cannot. If the router no longer receives updates, ask for a replacement.
What is it?

Cameras protect homes and shops — and, if hijacked, expose them. A secure camera has a changed password, current firmware, MFA on its app and no unnecessary remote access. A respectful camera covers only what it needs to, never private spaces of others, and people know it is there. Under the DPDP Act 2023, video of identifiable people is personal data.

A housing society installed eight cameras with an online viewing app and left the installer's default password. A resident's teenage son found the live feed listed on a website of exposed cameras. The committee changed all passwords, updated the recorder's firmware, removed public cloud sharing, moved one camera that overlooked a flat's balcony, and put up a notice.
What is it?

Smart speakers listen for a wake word; smart TVs record viewing habits; fitness bands record routes and health data; children's watches share location. Each has privacy settings that are rarely changed. Small Bluetooth trackers, meant for finding keys, can be misused to follow a person; modern phones can alert you to an unknown tracker travelling with you.
If an unknown tracker is found

Safety first: a tracker placed on someone may be part of stalking or domestic abuse. Note and photograph it and the phone alert; do not go home if the person feels unsafe; contact the police or 181. Disabling it may alert the person who placed it, so plan with the person and the police (Module 7).
What is it?

Smart-device incidents combine privacy, safety and evidence. Preserve first (screenshots of the app, the leaked page address, the tracker alert), then isolate and secure — and check every other device on the same network, because one weak device usually means others.
